newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: BT seeks more telecom partners in Asia - CEO.
newsitem.headline: BT seeks more telecom partners in Asia - CEO.

text.p: British Telecom will spend more time seeking strategic alliances in Asia, chief executive Peter Bonfield said on Wednesday.

"We want to spend more effort in setting up partnerships in Asia. We already have a very comprehensive set of partners in Europe and ... through MCI in the United States," Bonfield told reporters in Singapore.
BT and America's MCI Communications Corp have formed a global telecom alliance called Concert Plc.

Touching on BT's relationship with Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (NTT), Bonfield said the two have had a technological relationship for more than 10 years and he would like to see it develop further.
"Everybody knows it is no secret that we would like to do more with NTT in the region," he said.

BT has been trying to get NTT, Asia's largest telecom player, to join Concert instead of two other major rival alliances, namely Unisource led by AT&T Corp and Global One which includes France Telecom, Deustche Telekom and Sprint Corp.
Bonfield said BT's strategy would be to look at individual countries in the region as their respective telecommuncation industries open up.
Recent tie-ups in Asia include forming a joint venture in South Korea with Korea's Dacom Corp and another with Japan's Marubeni Corp to provide domestic and global telecom services.
Bonfield said while the Japanese market was clearly the "the largest market in the region", priority would go to markets where liberalisation has taken place.
Bonfield said BT has teamed up with NTT to bid for telecom licences in region including in Singapore.
BT and NTT will both hold around 20 percent each in a consortium which is bidding for a basic telecom licence in Singapore.
The other partners in the consortium are government-owned Singapore Technologies and utility company Singapore Power.
Bonfield said BT would be interested in getting a Singapore mobile licence in the future.
"In my view, in the future there will be less distinction between fixed lines and mobile ... we won't rule out mobile opportunities in the future," he said.
Bonfield said he was optimistic BT would make money in Singapore as it was liberalising and a "growth market".
He said there would be a lot of demand for advanced telecom services as Singapore pursued its "intelligent island" plan.
Singapore has unveiled ambitious plans to wire up the island through a broadband high-speed network called Singapore ONE by 2000.
